units.translation: i.e. I cannot stand upright, where the corrector wrote γρ. βάσιν [var. base] above, I cannot walk, to which the following words are suited: τρέχω δὲ χερσίν, οὐ ποδωκείᾳ σκελών [I run with my hands, not with swiftness of legs], which have the meaning not of standing but of moving. To this passage should be referred Phrynichus' note in Bekker's Anecdota p. 23, 12: ἀκταινῶσαι [to be unable to stand upright]: Aeschylus says "οὐκέτ᾽ ἀκταίνω" [I no longer stand upright] with barytone accent, as if to say I can no longer hold myself upright. From this it is not clear whether he read στάσιν [standing] or βάσιν [step]; but perhaps he read μήτ᾽ ἔτ᾽ ἀκταίνειν [no longer to stand upright].
where στάσις [strife] was added from Bamberger's conjecture: Kiehl preferred ἔρις [strife] in Mnemosyne new series vol. 2 p. 229, as Aeschylus elsewhere said ἔριν αἱματόεσσαν [bloody strife].
which the scholiast explains as ἀμφιβολία [ambiguity], this is not unclear.

where the scholiast says: ἐπεὶ παπυροφάγοι οἱ Αἰγύπτιοι [since the Egyptians are papyrus-eaters]; on which see Theophrastus, History of Plants 4, 9 and Dioscorides 1, 116. The sense therefore is, as Schütz pointed out, that the fruit of the papyrus is not superior to an ear of corn, i.e. outside the metaphor: the Egyptians are not stronger than the Argives.
The expression was included among the proverbs by Zenobius 2, 73 and other paroemiographers.
